Luke 1: Luke opens "in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea" (Luke 1:5), Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC. The writer addresses Theophilus; tradition names him Luke, Paul's companion and "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14).
Luke 2: A decree of Caesar Augustus (ruled 27 BC–AD 14) sends Joseph to Bethlehem when Cyrenius (Quirinius) was governing Syria (Luke 2:1–2). How this census fits with Josephus's date for Quirinius (AD 6) is debated.
Luke 3: John's preaching begins "in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" (Luke 3:1), about AD 28–29. Jesus is "about thirty years of age" (Luke 3:23).
Luke 4: After forty days in the wilderness, Jesus returns to Galilee, reads in the synagogue at Nazareth, and moves on to Capernaum.
Luke 5: By the lake of Gennesaret, Jesus calls Simon, James, and John, partners in a fishing business.
Luke 6: Jesus chooses twelve apostles on a mountain and teaches the crowd "in the plain" (Luke 6:17).
Luke 7: Jesus heals a centurion's servant at Capernaum and raises a widow's son at Nain, a village south of Mount Tabor.
Luke 8: Jesus travels through Galilee's towns with the twelve and several women, then crosses to the country of the Gadarenes.
Luke 9: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and wants to see him. After the transfiguration, Jesus sets out for Jerusalem through Samaria (Luke 9:51–52).
Luke 10: Jesus sends out seventy. The good Samaritan's story is set on the road from Jerusalem down to Jericho, and Jesus visits Martha and Mary.
Luke 11: On the journey, Jesus teaches the disciples to pray and eats at a Pharisee's house.
Luke 12: An "innumerable multitude" (Luke 12:1) gathers as Jesus travels toward Jerusalem.
Luke 13: Jesus is told of Galileans killed by Pilate at their sacrifices and of the tower in Siloam (Luke 13:1–4). He is warned that Herod Antipas wants to kill him.
Luke 14: Jesus eats on the sabbath at the house of a chief Pharisee.
Luke 15: Tax collectors and sinners draw near to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes murmur (Luke 15:1–2).
Luke 16: Jesus tells of the unjust steward and the rich man and Lazarus, as the Pharisees listen.
Luke 17: Jesus passes "through the midst of Samaria and Galilee" (Luke 17:11) and heals ten lepers.
Luke 18: As Jesus nears Jericho, a blind man begs by the way (Luke 18:35).
Luke 19: In Jericho, Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, receives Jesus. Jesus enters Jerusalem from the mount of Olives and weeps over the city.
Luke 20: In the temple, the chief priests, scribes, and Sadducees question Jesus.
Luke 21: Jesus foretells Jerusalem "compassed with armies" (Luke 21:20). Rome besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70. He teaches daily in the temple and lodges on the mount of Olives.
Luke 22: The feast of unleavened bread draws near. Jesus eats the Passover, prays on the mount of Olives, and is taken to the high priest's house.
Luke 23: Pilate sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who is in Jerusalem for the feast; that day Pilate and Herod become friends (Luke 23:7, 12). Jesus is crucified at Calvary.
Luke 24: On the first day of the week, the risen Jesus appears on the road to Emmaus and in Jerusalem, then is carried up near Bethany.
John 1: The Gospel does not name its author; it says it rests on the witness of "the disciple whom Jesus loved" (John 21:20, 24), whom early tradition identifies as John, writing at Ephesus late in the 1st century. John baptizes at Bethabara beyond Jordan (John 1:28).
John 2: Jesus attends a wedding at Cana in Galilee, then goes to Jerusalem for Passover. The temple had been under construction forty-six years (John 2:20), placing this about AD 27–28.
John 3: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, visits Jesus at night in Jerusalem. John the Baptist is baptizing at Aenon near Salim.
John 4: Jesus passes through Samaria and stops at Jacob's well near Sychar, below Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped.
John 5: At "a feast of the Jews" (John 5:1), Jesus heals a man at the pool of Bethesda by the sheep market in Jerusalem.
John 6: Near Passover (John 6:4), Jesus feeds five thousand by the Sea of Galilee and teaches in the synagogue at Capernaum.
John 7: Jesus goes up secretly to Jerusalem for the feast of tabernacles, in autumn, and teaches in the temple.
John 8: Jesus teaches in the temple treasury (John 8:20) after the feast of tabernacles.
John 9: Jesus heals a man born blind, who washes in the pool of Siloam.
John 10: Jesus walks in Solomon's porch at the feast of the dedication, "and it was winter" (John 10:22–23).
John 11: Jesus raises Lazarus at Bethany, about fifteen furlongs (under two miles) from Jerusalem (John 11:18), then withdraws to Ephraim near the wilderness.
John 12: Six days before Passover (John 12:1), Mary anoints Jesus at Bethany, and Jesus enters Jerusalem.
John 13: "Before the feast of the passover" (John 13:1), Jesus washes his disciples' feet at supper.
John 14: Jesus speaks to his disciples at the supper, ending with "Arise, let us go hence" (John 14:31).
John 15: Jesus' farewell teaching to the disciples continues.
John 16: Jesus' farewell teaching ends with "I have overcome the world" (John 16:33).
John 17: Jesus prays for his disciples before going out across the brook Cedron (John 18:1).
John 18: Jesus is arrested in a garden across the Kidron valley, questioned by Annas and Caiaphas, and taken to Pilate's judgment hall.
John 19: Pilate sits in judgment at the Pavement, Gabbatha, about the sixth hour on "the preparation of the passover" (John 19:13–14). Jesus is buried in a new tomb in a garden.
John 20: On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty. Jesus appears to the disciples that evening and to Thomas eight days later.
John 21: Jesus appears to seven disciples by the sea of Tiberias (the Sea of Galilee), named for the city Herod Antipas built about AD 20.
